claims.text: Accelerated coupled degradation in multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys at elevated temperature is driven by selective corrosion at phase boundaries.
The phase boundaries are prone to micro-galvanic corrosion under corrosive exposure at high temperature.
Localized phase-boundary corrosion weakens interfaces between the eutectic phases.
Weakening of interfaces between eutectic phases lowers resistance to mechanical wear.
Reduced interfacial wear resistance produces a synergistic increase in total degradation.
A targeted corrosion inhibitor will suppress localized corrosion at the phase boundaries.
Without inhibitor, corrosion preferentially degrades the phase boundaries.
Preferential phase-boundary degradation accelerates wear by increasing spalling and debris formation.
Suppressing corrosion at phase boundaries delays or mitigates mechanical wear.
Relative to the uninhibited baseline, inhibitor treatment will reduce the corrosion rate.
Relative to the uninhibited baseline, inhibitor treatment will reduce wear severity.
Relative to the uninhibited baseline, inhibitor treatment will reduce total coupled degradation.
The inhibitor and baseline conditions will use identical alloy samples and hold temperature, contact force, mechanical-wear conditions, and corrosive-medium composition constant.
Failure of inhibitor-treated samples to show a statistically significant reduction in both corrosion indicators and wear damage relative to the baseline will falsify the hypothesis.
